title: 7.6.10 Challenges: Make it yours
description: The game is complete. Change one rule of your own: a best score that survives a restart, a boss every fifth wave, or a Ship class that owns its own cooldown. Pick one; add an idea of your own on top if you like.

steps.title: Pick a rule and change it
steps.instructions:
Choose one of these three challenges. The check turns green when any one of them is in your code, so one is enough. An idea of your own is welcome on top of it. Start from the game in the editor. This game starts without the sound effects from 7.6.9; add them back if you like, but they are not required.

**Challenge 1: a best score (easy).** Keep a second variable called `best` that `startRound()` never resets. When a round ends (where `playing` becomes `false`), update `best` if the score beat it, and show it in `drawTop()` under the score. Press R: the score goes back to 0, and `best` stays.

**Challenge 2: a boss wave (medium).** In `makeWave()`, every fifth wave also gets a boss: `this.wave % 5 === 0` is true on waves 5, 10, 15 and so on. On those waves, push one more `new Enemy(...)` into the wave before it is returned, with 10 hp, half the wave's speed, and `boss.sprite.color = 'purple';` so it stands out. Because the boss is an `Enemy`, everything else already works.

**Challenge 3: a Ship class (hard).** Make `class Ship` with `this.sprite` and `this.cooldown`, and move `moveShip()` into it as `move()` and `fire()` into it as `fire()`. The list of shots belongs to the scene, so `fire()` *gives back* what it made: a new `Bullet` when Space is held and the cooldown is done, otherwise `null`. The scene keeps the list:

```js
const shot = ship.fire();
if (shot) bullets.push(shot);
```

`if (shot)` is false for `null` and true for a Bullet. Delete the old `cooldown` from the scene and reset `ship.cooldown` in `startRound()`.
hints: Whatever you pick, press R afterwards and check the game still starts cleanly.

steps.title: Name what you changed
steps.instructions: At the top of `script.js`, write one sentence as a `//` comment saying what your rule is and what would happen if you removed it.
hints: A rule is something the game decides. 'A boss comes every fifth wave' is a rule; 'I changed a colour' is not.

requirements.title: Your rule is in the code
requirements.description: One of the three challenges is there: a best score kept across rounds, a boss on every fifth wave (this.wave % 5 === 0), or a Ship class that owns this.cooldown. Help: 7.6.6 (Lab: A Spawner for the waves)

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "7.6.10 Challenges: Make it yours". The task they were given: The game is complete. Pick ONE of three challenges and add it (an idea of the student's own on top is welcome). Challenge 1, a best score: a variable best that startRound() never resets, raised when a round ends if the score beat it, and shown in drawTop(). Challenge 2, a boss wave: in makeWave(), on every fifth wave, push one more Enemy into the wave before it is returned, with 10 hp, half the wave's speed and a purple sprite. Challenge 3, a Ship class: a class Ship with its own this.sprite and this.cooldown, whose move() and fire() replace moveShip() and fire(), where fire() gives back a new Bullet or null and the scene pushes it. Then write one // comment at the top saying what the rule is. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. moSHion facts that matter here: setup() runs once; draw() runs about 60 times a second, and so does every function it calls. kb.presses('space') is true only on the one frame a key goes down; kb.pressing('space') is true on every frame it is held. y grows downward. In this game draw() calls the game's own functions every frame, inside if (playing) { ... }. sprite.delete() (its other name is remove()) takes a sprite off the screen, and array.splice(i, 1) takes it out of the array; a shot or enemy that is gone has to leave both the screen and the array. A loop that runs from the end of an array to the start never skips an item when one is spliced out. overlaps() asks whether two sprites touch right now and changes nothing; it works for sprites with collider 'none', and colliding() never sees such a sprite. drawTop() runs after the sprites are drawn, so its words sit on top; text drawn in draw() lands underneath the sprites. In Part C each game object is a class instance that keeps its sprite in this.sprite, so a touch test names the sprites (this.sprite.overlaps(e.sprite)), not the objects. The game's classes have their own remove() that deletes the sprite. A finished object stays in its list until the clear-up at the end of the frame; filter returns a NEW array of the items whose test is true, so removing the finished sprites has to happen before the filter, or those sprites are left behind on screen. A static property belongs to the class and is reached as ClassName.name. startRound() runs on every restart, so anything it sets goes back; a value that must survive R is set once, outside it. % gives the remainder, so wave % 5 === 0 is true on waves 5, 10 and 15. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable, parameter and helper-function names, template strings, arrow functions, a ternary or an if/else chain, x++ or x += 1 or x = x + 1, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Names that other code in the program already calls (startRound, makeWave, drawTop) must keep those names, because a renamed one is never called. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or a string never runs, and the STEP comments the starter came with are not the student's work. One challenge is enough for met; more than one is fine. The // comment from the second step is not this card. The starter has none of the three challenges: missing. Write each note for THIS student's own code, for a 14-year-old reader: short sentences, plain words. In a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Your rule is in the code
rubric.description: At least ONE of the three challenges really works in the code: (1) a best value that survives a restart (startRound() does not reset it) and is raised to the score when a round ends with a higher score (if (score > best) best = score, or Math.max, in any shape); (2) on every fifth wave (a % 5 test on the wave number, any shape) makeWave() adds one more Enemy to the array it returns; (3) a Ship class that keeps its own cooldown (this.cooldown) and does the moving or firing, with the scene using that class. Other numbers, colours or speeds than the suggested ones are fine. A best that startRound() sets back to 0 is not met: it never survives R. A boss that is built but never reaches the wave is not met. A different rule of the student's own, with none of the three, is partial: say this card looks for one of the three.
